title: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible orderings (permutations) using backtracking.
shortTitle: Permutations — backtracking with a used[] array

s1_definition.profdef: Build each permutation by choosing an unused element at every position via depth-first backtracking. A boolean used[] array marks elements already placed in the current path; when the path length equals n, record it as a complete permutation, then undo the choice to explore alternatives. This produces all n! orderings.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must try every order in which n settlement batches could run when order affects outcome. At each slot you pick a batch not yet used, fill all slots, record that full ordering, then unpick to try a different arrangement.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill positions one by one with unused elements; when full, record the ordering and backtrack — n! results.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Build each permutation by choosing an unused element at every position via depth-first backtracking. A boolean used[] array marks elements already placed in the current path; when the path length equals n, record it as a complete permutation, then undo the choice to explore alternatives. This produces all n! orderings.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India must try every order in which n settlement batches could run when order affects outcome. At each slot you pick a batch not yet used, fill all slots, record that full ordering, then unpick to try a different arrangement.

**One line to remember:** Fill positions one by one with unused elements; when full, record the ordering and backtrack — n! results.

sections.s2_technical:
Carry a path list and a used[] boolean array. When the path size equals n, record a copy. Otherwise loop over all indices, skip used ones, choose an element (mark used, append), recurse, then undo. For example: `if (used[i]) continue; used[i]=true; path.add(nums[i]); backtrack(); path.remove(last); used[i]=false;`.

Unlike subsets, there is no start index, because every position can draw from any unused element, which is what generates orderings rather than combinations.

The time is O(n · n!) because there are n! permutations, each of length n to copy. A senior nuance is the swap-based in-place variant that avoids the used[] array by swapping elements into position, trading clarity for a small constant-factor space saving.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a set of distinct end-of-day settlement batches can run in any order, and a simulation must evaluate every possible run order for risk. This is exactly how generating permutations works.

Problem 2 — Each batch appears exactly once per ordering, and every ordering must be distinct. This is exactly why a used[] array tracks placed batches and there is no start index.

The mini-project builds a `BatchOrderSimulator`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three batches: one, two, three.

Step 1: Position zero picks one, then position one picks two, then position two picks three, giving [1,2,3]; it is recorded and the recursion unwinds.

Step 2: Backtracking swaps the deeper choices to form [1,3,2], then the first position changes to two yielding [2,1,3] and [2,3,1], and finally three yielding [3,1,2] and [3,2,1].

Step 3: All six orderings are recorded, each batch used exactly once per ordering.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations is the backtracking problem for generating every ordering of distinct elements. I carry the current partial ordering plus a boolean used array, and whenever the path reaches length n I record a copy as a complete permutation. Otherwise I loop over every index, skip the ones already used, choose an unused element by marking it and appending it, recurse, and then undo both actions to explore the remaining arrangements.

The key structural difference from subsets is that there is no start index: every position is free to draw from any element not yet placed, which is precisely what produces orderings rather than combinations. The cost is O(n times n factorial), since there are n factorial permutations and copying each costs n.

In my project at National Bank of India, a simulation had to evaluate every possible run order of a small set of distinct end-of-day settlement batches to assess order-dependent risk, and this backtracking enumerated them cleanly with each batch used exactly once per ordering. If space is at a premium I mention the in-place swap variant that drops the used array by swapping elements directly into position.
